title: The animal that broke the rules
text: When the first platypus specimen arrived in Britain in 1799, scientists {{1}} convinced that the creature was a hoax stitched together from a duck and a beaver. Over two centuries later it still defeats the categories: {{2}} has a duck's bill, an otter's coat and a beaver's tail, and it is in many ways {{3}} living bridge between reptiles and mammals. It hunts with its eyes closed in murky rivers, {{4}} electroreceptors in the bill detect the faint muscle signals of shrimp, and those same organs allow the animal {{5}} dig and navigate in total darkness. Males defend themselves with venomous spurs, {{6}} do only a handful of other mammals, and in its egg-laying and low body temperature the species often resembles a reptile more {{7}} a mammal. When {{8}} full genome was sequenced in 2008, it confirmed what naturalists had suspected all along: the platypus simply never read the textbook.

gaps.explanation: Past plural 'be' with the plural subject 'scientists'.
'It' refers back to the platypus as the subject.

gaps.hint: article: in many ways ___ living bridge
gaps.explanation: First mention of a singular countable noun takes 'a'.
'Where' refers back to the rivers as the place.
'Allow someone to do' — the infinitive follows the object.

gaps.hint: conjunction: spurs, ___ do only a few mammals
gaps.explanation: 'As do …' — the comparative clause of agreement after the comma.
'More … than' — the second element of the comparison.

gaps.hint: possessive: when ___ full genome was sequenced
gaps.explanation: The genome belongs to the platypus: its genome.
